import Foundation.FirstOrder.Basic
import Mathlib.Order.Filter.Ultrafilter.Basic

namespace LO

namespace FirstOrder

section

universe u v

variable {L : Language.{u}} {μ : Type v}
 {I : Type u} (A : I → Type u)
 [s : (i : I) → FirstOrder.Structure L (A i)]
 (𝓤 : Ultrafilter I)

namespace Structure

structure Uprod (𝓤 : Ultrafilter I) where
  val : (i : I) → A i

instance UprodStruc : Structure L (Uprod A 𝓤) where
  func := fun _ f v => ⟨fun i ↦ (s i).func f (fun x ↦ (v x).val i)⟩
  rel  := fun _ r v => {i | (s i).rel r (fun x ↦ (v x).val i)} ∈ 𝓤

instance [Nonempty I] [(i : I) → Nonempty (A i)] : Nonempty (Uprod A 𝓤) := Nonempty.map (⟨·⟩) inferInstance

@[simp] lemma func_Uprod {k} (f : L.Func k) (v : Fin k → Uprod A 𝓤) :
    Structure.func f v = ⟨fun i ↦ (s i).func f (fun x ↦ (v x).val i)⟩ := rfl

@[simp] lemma rel_Uprod {k} (r : L.Rel k) (v : Fin k → Uprod A 𝓤) :
    Structure.rel r v ↔ {i | (s i).rel r (fun x ↦ (v x).val i)} ∈ 𝓤 := of_eq rfl

end Structure

namespace Semiterm

open Structure

variable (e : Fin n → Uprod A 𝓤) (ε : μ → Uprod A 𝓤)

lemma val_Uprod (t : Semiterm L μ n) :
    t.valm (Uprod A 𝓤) e ε = ⟨fun i ↦ t.val (s i) (fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i)⟩ :=
  by induction t <;> simp[*, val_func]

end Semiterm

open Structure

variable {A} {𝓤}

namespace Semiformula

variable {e : Fin n → Uprod A 𝓤} {ε : μ → Uprod A 𝓤}

lemma val_vecCons_val_eq {z : Uprod A 𝓤} {i : I} :
    (z.val i :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) = (fun x ↦ ((z :> e) x).val i) := by
  simp [Matrix.comp_vecCons (Uprod.val · i), Function.comp_def]

lemma eval_Uprod [(i : I) → Nonempty (A i)] {φ : Semiformula L μ n} :
    Evalm (Uprod A 𝓤) e ε φ ↔ {i | Eval (s i) (fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ} ∈ 𝓤 := by
  induction φ using rec' <;>
    simp [*, Prop.top_eq_true, Prop.bot_eq_false, eval_rel, eval_nrel, Semiterm.val_Uprod]
  case hverum => exact Filter.univ_mem
  case hnrel k r v =>
    exact Ultrafilter.compl_mem_iff_not_mem.symm
  case hand =>
    exact Filter.inter_mem_iff.symm
  case hor φ ψ ihp ihq =>
    exact Ultrafilter.union_mem_iff.symm
  case hall φ _ =>
    constructor
    · intro h
      let z : Uprod A 𝓤 := ⟨fun i =>
        Classical.epsilon (fun z => ¬Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ)⟩
      exact Filter.mem_of_superset (h z) (by
        intro i hι a
        have : Eval (s i) (z.val i :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ :=
          by rw [val_vecCons_val_eq]; exact hι
        by_contra hc
        have : ¬Evalm (A i) (z.val i :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ :=
          Classical.epsilon_spec (p := fun z => ¬(Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) _ φ)) ⟨a, hc⟩
        contradiction)
    · intro h x
      exact Filter.mem_of_superset h (by intro i h; simpa [val_vecCons_val_eq] using h (x.val i))
  case hex φ _ =>
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨x, hx⟩
      exact Filter.mem_of_superset hx (by intro i h; use x.val i; simpa[val_vecCons_val_eq] using h)
    · intro h
      let z : Uprod A 𝓤 := ⟨fun i =>
        Classical.epsilon (fun z => Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ)⟩
      use z
      exact Filter.mem_of_superset h (by
        intro i; rintro ⟨x, hx⟩
        have : Eval (s i) (z.val i :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ :=
          Classical.epsilon_spec (p := fun z => Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) _ φ) ⟨x, hx⟩
        rw[val_vecCons_val_eq] at this; exact this)

lemma val_Uprod [(i : I) → Nonempty (A i)] {φ : Formula L μ} :
    Evalfm (Uprod A 𝓤) ε φ ↔ {i | Evalf (s i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ} ∈ 𝓤 := by
  simp [Evalf, eval_Uprod, Matrix.empty_eq]

end Semiformula

lemma models_Uprod [Nonempty I] [(i : I) → Nonempty (A i)] {φ : SyntacticFormula L} :
    (Uprod A 𝓤) ⊧ₘ φ ↔ {i | (A i) ⊧ₘ φ} ∈ 𝓤 := by simp [models_iff₀, Semiformula.val_Uprod, Empty.eq_elim]

variable (A)

def Semiformula.domain [(i : I) → Nonempty (A i)] (φ : SyntacticFormula L) := {i | A i ⊧ₘ φ}

end

section

variable {L : Language.{u}} {T : Theory L}

abbrev FinSubtheory (T : Theory L) := {t : Finset (SyntacticFormula L) // ↑t ⊆ T}

variable (A : FinSubtheory T → Type u) [s : (i : FinSubtheory T) → Structure L (A i)]

instance : Nonempty (FinSubtheory T) := ⟨∅, by simp⟩

lemma ultrafilter_exists [(t : FinSubtheory T) → Nonempty (A t)]
    (H : ∀ (i : FinSubtheory T), (A i) ⊧ₘ* (i.val : Theory L)) :
    ∃ 𝓤 : Ultrafilter (FinSubtheory T), Set.image (Semiformula.domain A) T ⊆ 𝓤.sets :=
  Ultrafilter.exists_ultrafilter_of_finite_inter_nonempty _ (by
    haveI : DecidableEq (Set (FinSubtheory T)) := fun _ _ => Classical.propDecidable _
    intro t ht
    have : ∃ t' : Finset (SyntacticFormula L), ↑t' ⊆ T ∧ Finset.image (Semiformula.domain A) t' = t := by
      simpa [Finset.subset_set_image_iff] using ht
    rcases this with ⟨t, htT, rfl⟩
    exact ⟨⟨t, htT⟩, by
      suffices ∀ i ∈ t, A ⟨t, htT⟩ ⊧ₘ i by simpa [Semiformula.domain] using this
      intro i hi; exact (H ⟨t, htT⟩).RealizeSet hi⟩)

lemma compactness_aux :
    Satisfiable T ↔ ∀ i : FinSubtheory T, Satisfiable (i.val : Theory L) := by
  constructor
  · rintro h ⟨t, ht⟩; exact Semantics.Satisfiable.of_subset h ht
  · intro h
    have : ∀ i : FinSubtheory T, ∃ (M : Type u) (_ : Nonempty M) (_ : Structure L M), M ⊧ₘ* (i.val : Theory L) :=
      by intro i; exact satisfiable_iff.mp (h i)
    choose A si s hA using this
    have : ∃ 𝓤 : Ultrafilter (FinSubtheory T), Set.image (Semiformula.domain A) T ⊆ 𝓤.sets := ultrafilter_exists A hA
    rcases this with ⟨𝓤, h𝓤⟩
    have : Structure.Uprod A 𝓤 ⊧ₘ* T := ⟨by intro σ hσ; exact models_Uprod.mpr (h𝓤 $ Set.mem_image_of_mem (Semiformula.domain A) hσ)⟩
    exact satisfiable_intro (Structure.Uprod A 𝓤) this

theorem compact :
    Satisfiable T ↔ ∀ u : Finset (SyntacticFormula L), ↑u ⊆ T → Satisfiable (u : Theory L) := by
  rw[compactness_aux]; simp

instance : Compact (SmallStruc L) := by exact?

    intro t ht

      simpa [Finset.subset_set_image_iff] using ht

end Semiterm

open Structure

variable {A} {𝓤}

namespace Semiformula

variable {e : Fin n → Uprod A 𝓤} {ε : μ → Uprod A 𝓤}

lemma val_vecCons_val_eq {z : Uprod A 𝓤} {i : I} :

  simp [Matrix.comp_vecCons (Uprod.val · i), Function.comp_def]

  induction φ using rec' <;>
    simp [*, Prop.top_eq_true, Prop.bot_eq_false, eval_rel, eval_nrel, Semiterm.val_Uprod]
  case hverum => exact Filter.univ_mem
  case hnrel k r v =>
    exact Ultrafilter.compl_mem_iff_not_mem.symm
  case hand =>
    exact Filter.inter_mem_iff.symm
  case hor φ ψ ihp ihq =>
    exact Ultrafilter.union_mem_iff.symm
  case hall φ _ =>
    constructor
    · intro h
      let z : Uprod A 𝓤 := ⟨fun i =>
        Classical.epsilon (fun z => ¬Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ)⟩

        by_contra hc
        have : ¬Evalm (A i) (z.val i :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ :=

    · rintro ⟨x, hx⟩

    · intro h
      let z : Uprod A 𝓤 := ⟨fun i =>
        Classical.epsilon (fun z => Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ)⟩

      exact Filter.mem_of_superset h (by
        intro i; rintro ⟨x, hx⟩
        have : Eval (s i) (z.val i :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ :=
          Classical.epsilon_spec (p := fun z => Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) _ φ) ⟨x, hx⟩
        rw[val_vecCons_val_eq] at this; exact this)

  simp [Evalf, eval_Uprod, Matrix.empty_eq]

end Semiformula

lemma models_Uprod [Nonempty I] [(i : I) → Nonempty (A i)] {φ : SyntacticFormula L} :

      suffices ∀ i ∈ t, A ⟨t, htT⟩ ⊧ₘ i by simpa [Semiformula.domain] using this
      intro i hi; exact (H ⟨t, htT⟩).RealizeSet hi⟩)

    Satisfiable T ↔ ∀ i : FinSubtheory T, Satisfiable (i.val : Theory L) := by
  exact?

variable (e : Fin n → Uprod A 𝓤) (ε : μ → Uprod A 𝓤)

lemma val_Uprod (t : Semiterm L μ n) :
    t.valm (Uprod A 𝓤) e ε = ⟨fun i ↦ t.val (s i) (fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i)⟩ :=
  by induction t <;> simp[*, val_func]

end Semiterm

open Structure

variable {A} {𝓤}

namespace Semiformula

variable {e : Fin n → Uprod A 𝓤} {ε : μ → Uprod A 𝓤}

lemma val_vecCons_val_eq {z : Uprod A 𝓤} {i : I} :
    (z.val i :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) = (fun x ↦ ((z :> e) x).val i) := by
  simp [Matrix.comp_vecCons (Uprod.val · i), Function.comp_def]

lemma eval_Uprod [(i : I) → Nonempty (A i)] {φ : Semiformula L μ n} :
    Evalm (Uprod A 𝓤) e ε φ ↔ {i | Eval (s i) (fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ} ∈ 𝓤 := by
  induction φ using rec' <;>
    simp [*, Prop.top_eq_true, Prop.bot_eq_false, eval_rel, eval_nrel, Semiterm.val_Uprod]
  case hverum => exact Filter.univ_mem
  case hnrel k r v =>
    exact Ultrafilter.compl_mem_iff_not_mem.symm
  case hand =>
    exact Filter.inter_mem_iff.symm
  case hor φ ψ ihp ihq =>
    exact Ultrafilter.union_mem_iff.symm
  case hall φ _ =>
    constructor
    · intro h
      let z : Uprod A 𝓤 := ⟨fun i =>
        Classical.epsilon (fun z => ¬Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ)⟩
      exact Filter.mem_of_superset (h z) (by
        intro i hι a
        have : Eval (s i) (z.val i :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ :=
          by rw [val_vecCons_val_eq]; exact hι
        by_contra hc
        have : ¬Evalm (A i) (z.val i :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ :=
          Classical.epsilon_spec (p := fun z => ¬(Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) _ φ)) ⟨a, hc⟩
        contradiction)
    · intro h x
      exact Filter.mem_of_superset h (by intro i h; simpa [val_vecCons_val_eq] using h (x.val i))
  case hex φ _ =>
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨x, hx⟩
      exact Filter.mem_of_superset hx (by intro i h; use x.val i; simpa[val_vecCons_val_eq] using h)
    · intro h
      let z : Uprod A 𝓤 := ⟨fun i =>
        Classical.epsilon (fun z => Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ)⟩
      use z
      exact Filter.mem_of_superset h (by
        intro i; rintro ⟨x, hx⟩
        have : Eval (s i) (z.val i :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ :=
          Classical.epsilon_spec (p := fun z => Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) _ φ) ⟨x, hx⟩
        rw[val_vecCons_val_eq] at this; exact this)

lemma val_Uprod [(i : I) → Nonempty (A i)] {φ : Formula L μ} :
    Evalfm (Uprod A 𝓤) ε φ ↔ {i | Evalf (s i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ} ∈ 𝓤 := by
  simp [Evalf, eval_Uprod, Matrix.empty_eq]

end Semiformula

lemma models_Uprod [Nonempty I] [(i : I) → Nonempty (A i)] {φ : SyntacticFormula L} :
    (Uprod A 𝓤) ⊧ₘ φ ↔ {i | (A i) ⊧ₘ φ} ∈ 𝓤 := by simp [models_iff₀, Semiformula.val_Uprod, Empty.eq_elim]

variable (A)

def Semiformula.domain [(i : I) → Nonempty (A i)] (φ : SyntacticFormula L) := {i | A i ⊧ₘ φ}

end

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: Finset.subset_set_image_iff
C1_dependencies.content:
/-- If a `Finset` is a subset of the image of a `Set` under `f`,
then it is equal to the `Finset.image` of a `Finset` subset of that `Set`. -/
theorem subset_set_image_iff [DecidableEq β] {s : Set α} {t : Finset β} {f : α → β} :
    ↑t ⊆ f '' s ↔ ∃ s' : Finset α, ↑s' ⊆ s ∧ s'.image f = t := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    letI : CanLift β s (f ∘ (↑)) fun y => y ∈ f '' s := ⟨fun y ⟨x, hxt, hy⟩ => ⟨⟨x, hxt⟩, hy⟩⟩
    lift t to Finset s using h
    refine ⟨t.map (Embedding.subtype _), map_subtype_subset _, ?_⟩
    ext y; simp
  · rintro ⟨t, ht, rfl⟩
    rw [coe_image]
    exact Set.image_subset f ht

C1_dependencies.content:
/-- All propositions are `Decidable`. -/
noncomputable scoped instance (priority := low) propDecidable (a : Prop) : Decidable a :=
  choice <| match em a with
    | Or.inl h => ⟨isTrue h⟩
    | Or.inr h => ⟨isFalse h⟩

C1_dependencies.name: Set
C1_dependencies.content:
/-- A set is a collection of elements of some type `α`.

Although `Set` is defined as `α → Prop`, this is an implementation detail which should not be
relied on. Instead, `setOf` and membership of a set (`∈`) should be used to convert between sets
and predicates.
-/
def Set (α : Type u) := α → Prop

theorem exists_ultrafilter_of_finite_inter_nonempty (S : Set (Set α))
    (cond : ∀ T : Finset (Set α), (↑T : Set (Set α)) ⊆ S → (⋂₀ (↑T : Set (Set α))).Nonempty) :
    ∃ F : Ultrafilter α, S ⊆ F.sets :=
  haveI : NeBot (generate S) :=
    generate_neBot_iff.2 fun _ hts ht =>
      ht.coe_toFinset ▸ cond ht.toFinset (ht.coe_toFinset.symm ▸ hts)
  ⟨of (generate S), fun _ ht => (of_le <| generate S) <| GenerateSets.basic ht⟩

informal_proof:
To understand the compactness theorem, let's first clarify its meaning. A theory \( T \) in first-order logic is considered *satisfiable* if there exists at least one model that interprets all its sentences as true. The theorem establishes a crucial equivalence:

1. **Forward Direction**: If the entire theory \( T \) is satisfiable (i.e., there exists a model that satisfies all sentences in \( T \)), then every finite subset \( u \) of \( T \) must also be satisfiable. This is because any model that satisfies \( T \) will automatically satisfy any finite collection of sentences within \( T \), as being a subset of \( T \).

2. **Reverse Direction**: Conversely, if every finite subset of \( T \) is satisfiable, then the entire theory \( T \) is satisfiable. This follows from the compactness theorem in logic, which states that if every finite subset of a set of sentences has a model, then the entire set has a model. The idea is that models can be "glued" together from these finite satisfiable subsets to form a model for the entire theory \( T \).

Thus, the theorem establishes a deep connection between the satisfiability of infinite theories and their finite fragments, providing a powerful tool in model theory and logic. The equivalence holds because the compactness theorem ensures that the behavior of infinite theories can be understood through their finite components.

  induction φ using rec' <;>
    simp [*, Prop.top_eq_true, Prop.bot_eq_false, eval_rel, eval_nrel, Semiterm.val_Uprod]
  case hverum => exact Filter.univ_mem
  case hnrel k r v =>
    exact Ultrafilter.compl_mem_iff_not_mem.symm
  case hand =>
    exact Filter.inter_mem_iff.symm
  case hor φ ψ ihp ihq =>
    exact Ultrafilter.union_mem_iff.symm
  case hall φ _ =>
    constructor
    · intro h
      let z : Uprod A 𝓤 := ⟨fun i =>
        Classical.epsilon (fun z => ¬Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ)⟩
      exact Filter.mem_of_superset (h z) (by
        intro i hι a
        have : Eval (s i) (z.val i :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ :=
          by rw [val_vecCons_val_eq]; exact hι
        by_contra hc
        have : ¬Evalm (A i) (z.val i :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ :=
          Classical.epsilon_spec (p := fun z => ¬(Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) _ φ)) ⟨a, hc⟩
        contradiction)
    · intro h x
      exact Filter.mem_of_superset h (by intro i h; simpa [val_vecCons_val_eq] using h (x.val i))
  case hex φ _ =>
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨x, hx⟩
      exact Filter.mem_of_superset hx (by intro i h; use x.val i; simpa[val_vecCons_val_eq] using h)
    · intro h
      let z : Uprod A 𝓤 := ⟨fun i =>
        Classical.epsilon (fun z => Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ)⟩
      use z
      exact Filter.mem_of_superset h (by
        intro i; rintro ⟨x, hx⟩
        have : Eval (s i) (z.val i :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) (fun x ↦ (ε x).val i) φ :=
          Classical.epsilon_spec (p := fun z => Eval (s i) (z :> fun x ↦ (e x).val i) _ φ) ⟨x, hx⟩
        rw[val_vecCons_val_eq] at this; exact this)

informal_proof:
We aim to prove that a theory \( T \) is satisfiable exactly when every finite subset of \( T \) is satisfiable.

First, we consider the forward direction of the equivalence. Assume \( T \) is satisfiable. Then, any finite subset of \( T \) is also satisfiable, since any model of \( T \) is also a model of any of its finite subsets.

For the converse, assume that every finite subset of \( T \) is satisfiable. Our goal is to show that \( T \) itself is satisfiable. This is where the compactness theorem comes into play, which states that if every finite subset of a theory is satisfiable, then the entire theory is satisfiable.

To apply the compactness theorem, we consider the ultraproduct construction. Given the satisfiability of all finite subtheories, we can construct an ultraproduct using an appropriate ultrafilter. This ultraproduct will serve as a model for the entire theory \( T \), thereby demonstrating that \( T \) is satisfiable.

Thus, we have shown both directions of the equivalence, completing the proof.

Furthermore, for any finite set of such finite subtheories \( t \), the intersection of their corresponding \( A(t) \) sets is also nonempty. Therefore, there exists an ultrafilter \( \mathcal{U} \) on the set of finite subtheories of \( T \) such that for every finite subtheory \( t \), the set \( A(t) \) is an element of \( \mathcal{U} \).

To establish the existence of the desired ultrafilter \( \mathcal{U} \), we proceed as follows:

1. **Understanding the Setting**: We consider the set of all finite subtheories of a given theory \( T \). For each finite subtheory \( t \), the set \( A(t) \) is defined and is nonempty. Our goal is to extend this collection of sets into an ultrafilter.

2. **Finite Intersection Property**: An ultrafilter must satisfy the finite intersection property, meaning that the intersection of any finite number of sets in the ultrafilter is also in the ultrafilter. Given that for every finite subtheory \( t \), \( A(t) \) is nonempty, and considering that the intersection of finitely many nonempty sets remains nonempty under the classical definition of nonempty, we confirm that the finite intersection property holds.

3. **Application of the Ultrafilter Existence Lemma**: The lemma in question states that any family of sets with the finite intersection property is contained in some ultrafilter. Given that \( \{A(t)\}_{t} \) is such a family with the finite intersection property, we can apply this lemma.

4. **Conclusion**: By the Ultrafilter Existence lemma, there exists an ultrafilter \( \mathcal{U} \) on the set of finite subtheories of \( T \) such that \( A(t) \subseteq \mathcal{U} \) for every finite subtheory \( t \). This ultrafilter is the required \( \mathcal{U} \) that satisfies the conditions.

Therefore, the existence of such an ultrafilter is guaranteed by the Ultrafilter Existence lemma, and it is necessary because the finite intersection property ensures that the family can be extended to an ultrafilter. This selection of \( \mathcal{U} \) serves the purpose of capturing the essential properties of the system in an ultrafilteroretic manner.

The uniform product of \( A_i \) over an ultrafilter \( \mathcal{U} \) on \( I \) satisfies a formula \( \varphi \) if and only if the set of all indices \( i \) for which \( A_i \) satisfies \( \varphi \) is an element of \( \mathcal{U} \).
informal_proof:
We aim to show that the uniform product \( \prod_{\mathcal{U}} A_i \) satisfies the formula \( \varphi \) if and only if the set of indices \( I_\varphi = \{i \in I \mid A_i \models \varphi\} \) is in the ultrafilter \( \mathcal{U} \).

1. **Understanding Uniform Product**: The uniform product \( \prod_{\mathcal{U}} A_i \) is constructed by taking the Cartesian product of the families of sets weighted by the ultrafilter \( \mathcal{U} \). Elements of \( \prod_{\mathcal{U}} A_i \) are equivalence classes of functions \( f: I \to \bigcup A_i \) where \( f(i) \in A_i \), and two functions \( f \) and \( g \) are equivalent if \( \{i \in I \mid f(i) = g(i)\} \in \mathcal{U} \).

2. **Logical Consequence in the Uniform Product**: The statement \( \prod_{\mathcal{U}} A_i \models \varphi \) means that for every function \( f \) representing an element in \( \prod_{\mathcal{U}} A_i \), \( f \) satisfies \( \varphi \). Given the construction, this satisfaction is determined by the behaviors of the \( A_i \)s in a "large" subset of \( I \), as dictated by \( \mathcal{U} \).

3. **Characterization of \( I_\varphi \)**: The set \( I_\varphi \) contains all indices \( i \) where \( A_i \) individually satisfies \( \varphi \). To ensure that \( \prod_{\mathcal{U}} A_i \models \varphi \), a necessary condition is that the set \( I_\varphi \) is "large" enough, in the sense of being in \( \mathcal{U} \). This is because if most \( A_i \)s satisfy \( \varphi \), then any function \( f \) representing an element in \( \prod_{\mathcal{U}} A_i \) must have \( f(i) = \varphi \) for most \( i \), hence \( f \) globally satisfies \( \varphi \).

4. **Equivalence**: 
   - **Forward Direction**: Assume \( \prod_{\mathcal{U}} A_i \models \varphi \). This means every function \( f \) in \( \prod_{\mathcal{U}} A_i \) satisfies \( \varphi \). In particular, for almost all \( i \), \( A_i \) satisfies \( \varphi \), meaning \( I_\varphi \in \mathcal{U} \).
   
   - **Reverse Direction**: Assume \( I_\varphi \in \mathcal{U} \). Then, for any function \( f \) in \( \prod_{\mathcal{U}} A_i \), since \( f(i) \in A_i \) and \( A_i \models \varphi \) for \( I_\varphi \), we have \( f \) satisfies \( \varphi \) for most \( i \), hence \( f \) satisfies \( \varphi \) globally.

To understand this equivalence, let us begin by grasping the concept of an ultraproduct. An ultraproduct is a construction that combines a family of mathematical structures into a new structure, using an ultrafilter to specify which aspects of the component structures are "important" or "predominant" in the resulting structure. Intuitively, elements in the ultraproduct are sequences where most components " behave consistently" with respect to the ultrafilter.

The formula $\phi$ is a statement in a formal language, and saying that the ultraproduct $\prod_{\mathcal{U}} A_i$ satisfies $\phi$ means that $\phi$ holds true in this new, combined structure. On the other hand, the set $\{i \in I \mid A_i \text{ satisfies } \phi\}$ represents all the indices where the individual structures $A_i$ satisfy $\phi$. The ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ acts as a way to "emphasize" certain indices over others.

The equivalence stated in the problem can be intuitively understood as follows: if the ultraproduct $\prod_{\mathcal{U}} A_i$ satisfies $\phi$, it is because the ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ predominantly selects indices where $\phi$ holds across the component structures $A_i$. Conversely, if $\mathcal{U}$ predominantly contains the indices where each $A_i$ satisfies $\phi$, then the ultraproduct will naturally satisfy $\phi$ as well.

This relationship is significant because it bridges the behavior of individual structures to the behavior of their combination, offering a powerful tool to analyze properties across a family of structures using the properties of the individual members and the selector properties of the ultrafilter.

informal_statement: For every natural number \( n \), there exists a prime number \( p \) such that \( p \) is greater than \( n \). Equivalently, there are infinitely many prime numbers.
informal_proof:
Let \( n \) be an arbitrary natural number. We consider the number \( (n + 1)! + 1 \), where \( (n + 1)! \) denotes the factorial of \( n + 1 \). Since \( (n + 1)! \) is the product of all positive integers up to \( n + 1 \), \( (n + 1)! + 1 \) is at least 2, so it must have at least one prime factor, say \( p \).

Assume, for contradiction, that \( p \) is not greater than \( n \). Then, \( p \) is less than or equal to \( n \), which implies that \( p \) divides \( (n + 1)! \). Since \( p \) also divides \( (n + 1)! + 1 \), it must divide their difference, which is 1. This implies that \( p \) divides 1, which is impossible because the only divisor of 1 is 1 itself, and all prime numbers are greater than 1. This contradiction shows that our initial assumption is false, hence \( p \) must be greater than \( n \).

Therefore, for every natural number \( n \), there exists a prime number \( p \) such that \( p > n \), proving that there are infinitely many prime numbers.

We aim to show that for any two propositions \( a \) and \( b \), the conjunction \( a \land b \) is equivalent to \( b \land a \). To do this, we need to demonstrate both directions of the equivalence: that \( a \land b \) implies \( b \land a \) and that \( b \land a \) implies \( a \land b \).

First, assume that \( a \land b \) is true. By the definition of conjunction, this means that both \( a \) and \( b \) are true. Therefore, swapping their order, \( b \land a \) is also true because both \( b \) and \( a \) hold.

Conversely, assume that \( b \land a \) is true. Using the same reasoning, since both \( b \) and \( a \) are true, \( a \land b \) must also be true.

Since both directions hold for any propositions \( a \) and \( b \), we conclude that \( a \land b \) is equivalent to \( b \land a \).
